In the US and Canada, buttermilk is usually cultured buttermilk: skim or low-fat milk is soured with a mesophilic aroma culture and never churned.

cream.text: The cream spun out of the milk is far richer than any grade sold, so the dairy blends it back with skimmed milk until the fat hits the legal figure, then heats it. Grades differ by country and by use: coffee, whipping, double. Cream is heated like milk, but because fat shields bacteria it is held a little hotter once it reaches 10 % fat. Equivalent time-temperature pairs are allowed; the figures are the US legal definitions (21 CFR 131.3).

facts.v: Cream cheese, rather than the cottage cheese of earlier cheese pies
Eggs, baked (not set cold with cream or gelatin)
Ashkenazi Jewish cooking, 1930s New York (Gil Marks)

New York cheesecake.text: Cream cheese, sugar and eggs are mixed, poured on a crumb base and baked until the eggs set it; the cream cheese is what gives it the dense, creamy body. Cream cheese itself was only invented in the 1870s, so earlier cheese pies used cottage cheese.

facts.v: Anne Hov, 1863, in Gudbrandsdalen; the goat's milk was first added by Ole Steberg of Ringebu (original name Gudbrandsdalske blandingsost)
Tretten, 1908

Gudbrandsdalsost.text: Whey, milk and cream are boiled down carefully for several hours until the water has evaporated and the milk sugar has caramelised; goat's milk gives the stronger taste. No temperatures or times are given in the sources opened. Note: the 144 g figure is as written on no.wikipedia, which calls the goat milk 'pasteurisert geitemelk'; and it says cheese is whey + goat milk + cream + milk.

facts.v: Anne Hov, 1863, Valseter near Gålå: cream added to whey, boiled in an iron pot until the liquid was under 80 % (first called feitost)
Milder and lighter in colour than Gudbrandsdalsost; second most popular brunost in Norway

Fløtemysost.text: Cream and milk are added to the whey and the mix is boiled down for several hours until the water has gone and the milk sugar has caramelised. No goat's milk. No temperatures or times given in the sources opened.

cheesePowder.text: Cheese is minced, melted with water and emulsifying salts (usually phosphates) into a uniform "cheese feed", heated, often homogenised, and sprayed into hot air. Without the salts the hot cheese parts into fat and water, and the powder comes out coarse, dark and lumpy.
